It may be that the delays which the minister accuses the opposition of are of his own making because, as he knows or should know, there is a great deal of opposition in the country to the resolution now before the committee. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction not only among the manufacturers but also among those for whom the minister states this is going to be so helpful. I refer, of course, to those who are manufacturers of textiles.
I should like to go back to the textile industry and inquire of the minister what the government has been doing to help them. First of all let us take a look at the position. Mr. W. M. Berry, president of the Primary Textiles Institute, made a statement before the Senate committee on manpower the other day and he is quoted as saying;
Imported textiles cost 35,000 jobs in the Canadian textile industry last year and the situation is going to get worse unless something is done.
He presented a brief to the committee on manpower wherein there was a complaint that foreign made fabrics were already outselling Canadian made products in the home markets and in which it was said that if the present situation continued another 14,000 textile workers would be out of their jobs before 1970. I will not deal at further length with what was said by the president of the institute before the manpower committee, but I should like to know and I think the house is entitled to know from the minister what has been done by the government to come to the assistance of this industry.
The minister may be aware that in the last but one issue of the Financial Post there was a section dealing with industry in the province of Quebec and a portion of that section was devoted to the textile industry. As the minister knows, textiles are a very important industry in the province of Quebec. Mr. Eric Richter, who writes in the Financial Post, stated in the issue of February 4 last:
Quebec's big, important textile industry is struggling hard to hang on. For most of the provinces 370-odd mills and establishments, 1960 results were disappointing, even when measured against the lean years the textile industry has had in the past decade.

Customs Tariff
Then he went on to make this very important statement:
Recent redefinition of "class and kind not made in Canada"-
As outlined in the resolution now before us.
-for customs duty purposes doesn't help the textile industry much. It is already making just about every variety of textile products that can be economically produced.
Here is one person, along with many others, who feels that this provision is not going to be of a great deal of use. I come back to the discussion we had the last time this matter was up for consideration and I should like to ask the minister a question. It has to do with the statement made by the Prime Minister in the city of Cornwall on February 25, 1958, when he stated that he "saw no reason why protection cannot be provided for the textile industry". Then he added:
"We acted to protect the farmers against dumping of agricultural products in this country because we believed it unjust and unfair that the Canadian farmer should be subjected to unfair competition." The Prime Minister followed by explaining he could see no reason why the textile industry would not be treated in the same way.
My question, of course, is this. In the light of that statement made by the Prime Minister, I ask the minister what has been done by the government, by the Minister of Finance or by the Minister of National Revenue to implement this promise. I should not like the minister to create a diversion as he did the other day by asking me what I would do. As the house knows, it is the responsibility of the government in office to take the necessary steps to deal with a situation which is serious and acute. It is the government's responsibility in the light of the statement made by the Prime Minister. But for fear that again I shall be placed in the position of being accused of attacking without offering any alternative and having the minister say to me, "Well, what would you have done?" I will tell him in advance using some of the comments I made in a speech in French which I delivered on the subject matter. I should now like to put those remarks on Hansard.
(Translation):
On that occasion, I said this: It is surprising that, so far, all the attention has been centred on customs duties as if there was no other method likely to assist the manufacturing section of our industry.
That sector needs the intervention of the government because its production costs are too high to enable it to compete with foreign producers on the domestic market.

We have been suggesting for a long time, Mr. Chairman, that production costs are too high and that the government takes little or no action to help this manufacturing industry to compete with foreign industry.
The immediate result of tariff protection is to increase the price of foreign products and not to lower the price of domestic products.
It seems that the main purpose of the government's intervention in this field should be to bring about a decline in production costs so as to enable our manufacturing industry to face competition. In many instances, costs could be reduced if our production were first of all, more specialized and had access to wider markets.
Such increased specialization would require a more or less extended period of adjustment, according to the special conditions in each industry.
Second, during that period, the government would implement a varied and flexible assistance program likely to meet the concrete requirements of our various industries.
Third, this program could be made up of:
(a)	long term loans;
(b)	special grants;
(c)	specific tax exemptions; and
(d)	credit for development.
Other formulas might also be used as, for example, accelerated depreciation. What is most important is that the program must be flexible and well adjusted to the concrete conditions in each industry. It should therefore be implemented in close co-operation with the representatives of labour and of industry.
In brief, Mr. Chairman, societ competition, the necessity of helping underdeveloped countries, the shaping up of regional groups in Europe, the re-awakening of protectionist forces in North America, in the United States as well as in Canada, are, to my mind, a challenge to the western world and, more particularly, to Canada, which though it cannot stand alone, refuses to be finally integrated into the American economy.
The most satisfying answer to that challenge in the economic as well as in the political field, is, I think, to come as early as possible to an agreement with regard to the gradual setting up of an Atlantic economic community.
If, as I said before, our country promoted that concept at the next meeting of the O.E.E.C., of which it is now a member, it would serve not only our best interests, but also those of the free world.

(Text):
I come back now to the question I asked the minister earlier. What has been done by the government to implement the promise made by the Prime Minister in the statement he made on February 25, 1958, and which I outlined earlier?

May I ask the
hon. member a question before he sits down?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

In the recommendations the hon. member has just put forward there was no mention whatsoever of any increase in tariffs or any other protection for the textile industry. Furthermore no tariff assistance or increased protection was given to the textile industry by the former government when they were in power and therefore I take it that the hon. member for Laurier or erstwhile member for Stormont was at that time either not in favour of increased tariffs or did not have sufficient influence with his colleagues in order to have this result brought about. Is he now or was he in favour of an increase in tariffs to protect the cotton industry?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend will read what I have put on Hansard, then he will get his answer.
I have read it. I have followed what the hon. member has just said and there has been no reference whatever to any increase in tariff protection. I assume, then, he is not in favour of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then, will the hon. member tell me what I said?
I cannot say in detail what the hon. member said, but his remarks were directed toward subsidies, tax exemptions or export credits. There was no mention whatever of any increase in tariffs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I may deal with the hon. member's question, Mr. Chairman, and the committee will endure it, the position-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member is speaking from a lofty height.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Not any loftier than the hon. member who interrupted because, after all, who does he think he is? If the hon. member wants to take part in the debate, he may do so. I do not believe he has any right to interrupt, from his seat, a member who has the floor.
I have been asked a question and I propose to deal with it unless the Chairman calls me to order. The question that was asked concerned what I would have advocated in
Customs Tariff
connection with the textile mills in Cornwall. I have already put that information on record and I do not intend to repeat it. This statement does not deal with tariff protection because, as I have stated here and as I repeat now, in my opinion that is not the method with which to deal with the situation. In any event, here is a clear promise made by the Prime Minister of this country to the textile workers of Cornwall to deal with the situation. I am asking the minister now, what was done by the government to implement the promise of the Prime Minister? Since this government has been in office, not only has the production of the textile industry gone down substantially but, according to Mr. Berry, no less than 35,000 jobs have been lost to textile workers. As my friend the hon. member for Stormont knows, or should know if he is awake to the situation, no less than three industries have closed in Cornwall.

The answer was somewhat ambiguous, but from what the hon. member has said I take it that neither is he nor are his colleagues in favour of any form of increased tariff protection for the textile industry.
Are you?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What about you? Are you?
Yes, personally I am definitely in favour of it. Is the hon. member and his colleagues in favour of it?
What about your government?

The resolution before the committee, if finally enacted by parliament, will mean a drastic increase in tariffs in this country. The minister has complained rather bitterly on various occasions that the opposition are delaying the passage of this measure. He has suggested that we are conducting something of a filibuster.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.
The minister has used that very word during questions on orders of the day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; these words were applied to the official opposition.
The minister has amended his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no; it was very clear they applied to the Liberal opposition.
The minister has amended his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, he has not
amended them.

In my judgment, any opposition to this measure is well founded and is in the

Customs Tariff
interests of the people of this country. To the extent that both opposition parties use the forum of the House of Commons to point out the weaknesses of this measure they will be serving the people of Canada. I do not believe there is any doubt about the fact that the adoption of this measure will mean a drastic general increase in tariffs. After all, if that would not be the result, why would the government be introducing this measure?
There are in the measure important provisions which will mean an increase in tariffs. The main one is perhaps the redefinition of the provision relating to goods of a class or kind produced in Canada. This particular paragraph reads as follows:
Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom made to specifications shall be deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least 10 per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
The addition of the word "approximately" of course widens the scope of this particular section drastically. The minister has said that in the judgment of the government this amendment is necessary because the tariff board and the courts in the last 10 years have rendered decisions that have not maintained the original purpose of this clause. What that addition means, of course, is that the government are not satisfied to take the definition of the courts and other legal bodies involved, but that they want to change the rules. They want to make a new set of rules which they hope will result in a much wider interpretation of this provision, thus enabling the government to go merrily along bringing about general increases in tariffs. This, of course, is one of the bad features of the resolution.
Another bad feature of this measure is the provision stating that a decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
This provision amounts to the minister's taking unto himself the power of lawmaking. The cabinet minister involved will make these decisions, and there will be no appeal to the tariff board or to the courts. This is the very dictatorial feature of this legislation. This particular feature of this measure is the opposite of good democratic government and flies in the face of everything the Minister of Finance stood for during his many years in opposition. I am certain, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian people do not like these arbitrary powers placed in the hands of a

minister. They did not like arbitrary powers being placed in the hands of ministers in the previous administration and they will not be happy about nor, in our judgment, will they support the placing of these arbitrary powers in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue.
As has already been pointed out, the minister has the right to decide what the Canadian consumption of certain goods is at a given time. By this means he will decide also what 10 per cent of that quantity will be. The minister, by this arbitrary decision, will decide the effect of the law as applied to a given industry. The minister has the further power to decide whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of certain goods within a reasonable period of time. I feel that the minister should come clean with the committee. I think he should be frank with the committee.
When this matter was being debated on a former occasion, the minister was asked the value of the commodities that would be affected by this legislation. He is asking parliament for sweeping powers to increase tariffs; he is asking for arbitrary powers which fly in the teeth of basic democratic rights. Yet when he is asked for an estimate of the value of the commodities to which this sweeping legislation would apply, his answer is, "I cannot make an estimate." The minister does not know, so he says. My opinion is that the minister knows only too well that the powers for which he is asking in this legislation will mean a widespread increase in tariffs affecting goods of great value, and the minister for this reason refuses to give parliament an estimate of the goods involved. The minister has made it abundantly clear in his own words that by this legislation, he wants to go back to the position of some ten years ago. What he is saying is that he has no faith in the positions taken by the tariff board and by the courts in the last ten years, and that he wants to change the rules by this amendment.
I think the government is on dangerous ground not only because this kind of legislation is unjustified and undesirable in an economic sense, but because it would seem to me that it opens up the whole question of retaliation under GATT. It seems to me that the government is endeavouring to do by an underhanded method that which it does not dare to do by an open method, namely the increasing of tariffs. The government is going back in my judgment to the days of R. B. Bennett. I know that when members say that this means a return to the days of R. B. Bennett, the minister is extremely sensitive and responds with a statement that the days of R. B. Bennett

were not so bad after all. In the view of the Canadian public, any return to the high tariffs of the R. B. Bennett days of 1930 will be a great mistake from which both the country and the present government will suffer.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Revenue has used in my opinion a lame excuse for assuming these arbitrary and sweeping powers. As reported at page 1718 of Hansard he made the following assertion:
This parliament itself is the high court. This is the court of appeal in which we are standing at the moment. This is the court of parliament to which the minister is responsible; and if any minister committed one per cent of the improprieties to which the hon. gentleman referred this morning the matter would certainly be brought to public attention; there would be discussion and debate in the House of Commons, a matter of public record, and no minister who had any sense of responsibility not only to his own office but to his colleagues and to his government would consider doing such things as was suggested. As I say, this is the final court of appeal, and it is one to which every minister is responsible.
Mr. Chairman, that statement may sound like a reasonable thing when people who are not aware of the workings of the House of Commons read it, but it is impossible for members of parliament to find out the basis on which the Minister of National Revenue will make his decisions. It is impossible for members of parliament to find out why the minister made certain decisions. As a matter of fact the government is saying that the minister is being given these arbitrary powers because he has information which is confidential, which he wants to keep confidential and which he will hide from the House of Commons; and it is saying that no matter how many motions for production of papers that members may put on the order paper; no matter how we may try to ferret out the information in regard to the reasons why the minister makes certain arbitrary decisions that information will be hidden from parliament. It will be said that it is not in the public interest to disclose it which usually means that it is not in the political interest of the Conservative party.
Mr. Chairman, in years gone by we have heard in the strongest possible terms a condemnation by the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Eglinton-he was sitting in the opposition at the time-in regard to the grave injustice which flows from arbitrary powers. Under this legislation the Minister of National Revenue, will have all of the arbitrary powers that the Right Hon. C. D. Howe in the former administration was accused of having. This government rode to power to a very substantial degree on the argument that the former administration had taken arbitrary and dictatorial powers. That
Customs Tariff
is precisely what this government is doing in this legislation. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that such arbitrary powers are repugnant in a democratic nation.
I think this resolution should be opposed because it is high tariff protectionism. This legislation is the answer of the Conservative government to certain financial friends in certain big corporations who wanted this kind of protective legislation in order to make fabulous profits. This is the pay-off, in my judgment, of the Conservative party to certain financial interests in this nation and it has nothing whatsoever to do with the welfare of the Canadian public. I think it is a mistake for the government to turn the clock back. I think any general increase in tariffs as provided in this resolution will mean an increase in costs to Canada, a reduction in Canadian trade and a lower standard of living. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, we in this group intend to vote against this motion and against this legislation at every opportunity.

I have a number of notes here in connection with this matter, Mr. Speaker, but since the debate has been going on for several days now I will make my remarks as brief as possible.
I should like to say, however, that I support this resolution to amend the Customs Tariff most wholeheartedly. I am not an authority on customs tariffs, but I have had considerable experience in this regard in industry in my riding. I am quite satisfied that at the present time there is room for reclassification of a great many items, some of which are not made in Canada which come in duty free, and some of which are made in this country but whose component parts are imported from other countries duty free. At this time when Canadian industries are clamouring for new products to manufacture, I can name quite a few myself that would be made in this country if the normal protection of the Canadian customs tariff were provided, and it should be provided. I might make reference to heavy chains which are used for ships, in mines and in the construction industry. These chains come into Canada at the present time duty free because they are not made in Canada. I should like to remind you, Mr. Chairman, that during the first and second wars those chains had to be made in Canada and were made to a very large extent by hand. Following the end of the two wars there was no change made in the classification and the production of these chains in Canada ceased. At the present time I know of a Canadian chain manufacturer who is prepared to go into the production of these chains if there is a

Customs Tariff
reclassification which will give him the normal protection of the Canadian tariffs.
I might also give a similar example in regard to tire chains for heavy tractors. These tractors are used in the logging industry, in construction and in mines. Those chains now enter this country duty free and if they were reclassified these also would be made in Canada in larger quantities than they are made at the present time.
I might also mention the manufacture of automatic transmissions for automobiles. Since automatic transmissions came into use in Canadian cars or trucks they have all been made in the United States; but automatic transmissions have been installed in Canadian cars to such an extent that it would now be profitable to make them in Canada. However, there is no encouragement for General Motors or for Ford to have them made in Canada when they can bring them in duty free or under a customs drawback. I know for a fact that if adjustment were made in the Customs Tariff certain companies would be prepared to make automatic transmissions in Canada. In fact, negotiations are under way at the present time.
I have mentioned, in my way, three different items whose manufacture here would create a great deal of work if they were given the normal protection of the Customs Tariff. How hon. members opposite can read into this resolution signs that there is to be a general increase in tariff, I find difficult to understand. There is no indication here that such a thing will take place, or that tariffs will go sky high as some hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think. Here there is only a reclassification of certain things which are not made in Canada and certain things which are made in Canada but not enjoying the full benefit of the Customs Tariffs.
The part of the resolution which seems to have provoked the sharpest criticism is that which gives the Minister of National Revenue power to make reclassification. But to whom could such power better be given? You can always get to the minister, but you cannot get fast decisions from the tariff board.
Exactly.

I may say that only recently I had reason to make for one of our local industries an appointment with the tariff board on the subject of reclassifications. We were told that the tariff board was so busy with reports and recommendations that it would not be able to look into the matter for at least a year and maybe even longer. We must be realistic about these things. We must cut out much of the red tape and bring this thing down to where it belongs. Suppose

anyone objects to the decision of the minister. He can turn directly to his member of parliament or to the minister himself, and what could be better than that?
Oh, oh.

It would get right to the heart of the problem. As I said, there were other matters I hoped to deal with at this time, but may I conclude by saying that in principle I approve of this resolution. If it goes into effect I am sure that it will be the means of creating many new jobs for Canadians. In my opinion it is not going to cause any general increase in tariff, as the opposition seem to think it will. I may say that I myself would not be in favour of any such general increase.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Might I have a reply to the question I asked the minister a while ago, namely, what has the government done to implement the promise of the Prime Minister which I put on record?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, may I offer a correction of some impressions which the hon. member for Laurier evidently harbours. He seems to attribute to my trip to the west the fact that this debate has not been resumed since we were last engaged upon it on February 15. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that the trip to the west occurred prior to that date. Most of the travelling was done over a week end when the house was not in session, so it had no connection whatsoever with the fact that this debate was not resumed until today. The principal reason was that we had a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday of last week and a dominion-provincial conference on Thursday and Friday. It still is a fact that at dominion-provincial fiscal conferences the Minister of Finance is expected to be in attendance.
As to the question asked by the hon. member for Laurier about the textile industry, I would think, Mr. Chairman, that if you were disposed to make a ruling this matter probably lies outside the scope of the present discussion; but if you think it proper I shall be glad to deal with this subject. The hon. member for Laurier asks what the government has done to assist the textile industry. That, of course, takes us outside the scope of the resolution but I am entirely prepared to deal with this subject if you think it is proper in relation to this particular amendment. We have been engaged upon it for a long time and I do not wish to provide any hon. member with an excuse for going outside it and starting a debate on other matters rather than the class or kind definition. Perhaps, for the

sake of answering the hon. gentleman's question, I might just touch very lightly on this subject.
The first thing which was done was to refer the whole textile schedule in the Customs Tariff to the tariff board for review, and the tariff board has conducted an extensive inquiry over several years as a result of which it has made a series of reports. The first report involved recommendations for amendment of the Customs Tariff in respect of the importation of woollen fabrics. We brought to the house legislation to implement that recommendation and the house adopted it over the strong opposition of the hon. gentleman and those who sit with him. Since that time reports have been brought forward affecting other textile items in the Customs Tariff. Various changes have been made. In all cases in which the rates were bound under GATT, these rates have been negotiated with those countries in whose favour the bindings had been entered upon. In all respects the provisions of GATT have been strictly adhered to. One could mention as well the course of discussions at the GATT conference at the present time in the process of renegotiation there.
I remind the house also of the steps which have been taken during discussions with the representatives of the Japanese government in relation to imports of textile products from that country and the measures which have been taken as a result of those negotiations with a view to avoiding a repetition of the kind of concentration that occurred in the export of certain textile products to this country by Japanese firms. In the course of these discussions there has been consultation with the Canadian producers in the areas affected.
I remind the house also of the important amendments which we introduced in 1958 to the Customs Act dealing with the basis of valuation for duty purposes. Again, these were matters of great and urgent importance to the textile industry, but the amendments which were introduced by the government were sternly opposed by the hon. gentleman and those who sit with him. I need not remind the house, I am sure, of the exercise by the Minister of National Revenue of the powers he holds under the Customs Act-powers, incidentally, which existed in the time when the hon. gentleman was a minister of the crown-under which the flooding of the Canadian market by grey goods from China was avoided. I might mention also the present legislation in so far as the dumping of textile products into this country from other countries will be affected, because dumping, as I have reminded the committee in the course
Customs Tariff
of the discussion of this resolution on previous days when it has been before us, arises only in the case of goods of a class or kind made in Canada. That is why this present subject is of great importance to the whole question of dumping.
These are just a few of the measures which the government has taken. One could enlarge upon them. One could add to them. But if one did so it would be quite clear, I think, that we would be going outside the scope of this present debate.
The hon. member then spoke of a statement attributed to Mr. Berry, the general secretary of the Primary Textiles Institute of Canada, in which he said that imports of textiles into Canada have cost 35,000 jobs. I presume he was speaking in the sense that Canadian mills could have produced the particular textile goods to which he referred, and that had they done so 35,000 jobs would thereby have been created. He was not comparing employment in the textile industry today with what it was last year, the year before, or the year before that.
The fact is that the whole employment figure in the textile industry has not varied very much over the past several years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It has gone down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been very little variation. After all, the textile industry in Canada is a series of industries, and in the past several years some have done better and some have not done as well. It is probably better, in the interests of accuracy, to discuss a particular condition in a particular section of the industry and not to attempt to generalize for the whole industry in all its various parts.
My final observation relates to the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. Here again he was labouring under a complete misapprehension as to the nature of the amendment now under debate. He said the adoption of this amendment will mean large increases in tariffs. He said later it will mean widespread increases in tariffs. I must remind the committee that this is not the fact at all; there is not one single rate to be changed.
This measure does not propose to change one single rate in the Customs Tariff. It is simply concerned with a matter of definition, the definition of an expression that appears very frequently in the Customs Tariff. To see the amendment in its true proportions it is necessary to recall that what is proposed here is simply the restoration of what had been a well established interpretation before the decisions of the tariff board and courts in the past decade.
Another quite erroneous assertion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia was that

Customs Tariff
under this proposed amendment the Minister of National Revenue would take on the right to make law. This assertion is utterly without foundation. The minister has certain functions that he must discharge in relation to these questions, and the powers that the minister has been given under this legislation-
"Will be given".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-or will be given -you can take it either way you wish-are not nearly as extensive as are those parliament has conferred upon the minister in many, many other respects, not just in relation to this matter, but many others under legislation passed over the years by this parliament and now in effect.
This amendment concerns simply the question of definition. The hon. member was utterly mistaken when he said that this would give offence under GATT. I must remind him, I have said it several times already in the course of debate, that this question does not give rise to any question of GATT or bindings under GATT. These GATT bindings of particular rates were entered into years ago on the basis, so far as Canada is concerned, of the accepted interpretation of class or kind prevailing at that time. The definition and the interpretation were not bound. They are not the subject of a binding under GATT whatsoever. Therefore assertions that this action will lead to retaliation by other GATT countries falls completely to the ground; they are completely groundless.
As to the assertion that this measure would confer upon my colleague the Minister of National Revenue arbitrary powers, I must take firm issue with any such observation. Reference has been made to what I have said in this house in the past in regard to arbitrary powers. Believe me, Mr. Chairman, if I thought that arbitrary powers were proposed by the measure to be conferred upon my colleague the Minister of National Revenue, I would have done everything in my power to have prevented that objective being furthered. But that is not the fact. These are not arbitrary powers at all. These are necessary powers in the transaction of the business of this country.

Would the minister permit a question at this point? Would the minister not agree that every time an act or piece of legislation is passed in which it is said, "the decision of the minister shall be final", one is conferring arbitrary power? That is the definition of "arbitrary power".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think you have to look at all of the circumstances in a situation of this kind-
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and we must ask ourselves what is the reasonable view to take of the situation-
That is what all tyrants say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-and not run off
with catch phrases. I have said that I yield to no one in this house in my concern regarding arbitrary powers, and I put before the house my view that this is not at all the case of conferring arbitrary powers as has been pictured in observations such as those which fell from the mouth of the hon. member for Assiniboia this afternoon.
This legislation does not take away the right of appeal; the right of appeal continues. What is proposed in the amendment before the house is that in the appeal, in respect of three elements, the decision of the minister is final. We have been over this matter before. There is the question of the reasonableness, the necessity indeed, in the general interest of making provision that in those three cases the decision of the minister should be final. The right of appeal is taken away from no one. The most that can be said is that the right of appeal cannot be invoked on grounds that lie within the three points on which the Minister of National Revenue is given the right to make the final decision.
What are these three points? We have been over them before and I will not delay the committee on them now. The first is, that he can determine the normal Canadian consumption for other than custom-made goods. In other words, he can determine the normal consumption of what we call shelf goods. Surely that is eminently a decision for the minister.

Would the minister permit a factual question on this point? Would the minister tell us how that determination is going to be made before a decision is made as to what goods are approximately like the other goods in question? How can you determine the normal Canadian consumption of something until you know what that something is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I contemplate no difficulty over that matter.
Then please answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question that has been raised by the hon. member is presumably one that arises in an appeal.
It arises in administration also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An appeal is taken on the question he has raised. There is a right of appeal-

Mr. Chairman, would the minister allow me to make it clear. I was not raising the question with respect to appeals; I was raising it with respect to administration. I should like to know how this is going to be done, and I think the taxpayer would like to know also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the first instance when it becomes necessary for the minister to make a decision, he will certainly make a decision on those elements on which an appeal can be taken, as well as on those elements where an appeal will not lie. When he is making his decision, of course he will make it on whether the goods in question, being shelf goods, are approximately of the same class or kind as are now made in Canada.
He makes his determination on that element. He also makes his determination on Canadian production; he makes his determination on Canadian consumption, of course. Then in the event of appeal, an appeal can be taken against his decision as to whether or not the goods in question are of approximately the same class or kind as goods made in Canada. An appeal can lie on that question, and an appeal will lie against his determination with respect to the amount of Canadian production. There can be an appeal on that matter. There can similarly be an appeal on the question whether or not the number of articles manufactured in Canada does in fact constitute a minimum of 10 per cent of normal Canadian consumption. With respect to the other matter, the one I was speaking of, namely what is the normal Canadian consumption of shelf goods, his decision on that matter stands, and the appeal can proceed on the other question upon which the right of appeal continues unimpaired. I think this matter is quite clear, Mr. Chairman. I have touched on those matters upon which the right of appeal is clearly preserved and on those matters upon which finality is given to the decision of the minister for clear and good reason.
I am at this point introducing nothing new. Everything I am saying I said in the debate of earlier days on this present resolution. The amendments are designed to meet statistical problems in this regard in relation to the finality of the decision of the minister, and they are designed to permit cases involving class or kind articles to be resolved within a reasonable period of time. How highly important that is to the transaction of business. We have seen appeals that have dragged and dragged. They may involve questions
Customs Tariff
that apply to situations other than those directly involved in the appeal itself. This has had an embarrassing and oftentimes costly effect by reason of the delays caused. In the interest of better administration we are trying here to bring about the termination of these long and costly delays.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not satisfied with the answer which the minister has given to the question I put to him earlier. In my opinion two matters are involved here. The first is the statement of the Prime Minister that he would deal with the dumping of textile goods in the same way as the government dealt with the dumping of agricultural goods. In his reply the minister set out a list of the things that supposedly had been done to assist the textile industry. One of those was the reference of the whole matter to the tariff board. He referred to a return having to do with woollen fabrics. I should like to tell the Minister of Finance that there are no woollen mills in Cornwall and therefore this legislation would not be of any use to that community.
Then, he also referred to the legislation which was brought down in 1958. I ask the minister whether that legislation was actually used. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue, who is now in his seat-I presume he was detained earlier-will answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That matter was dealt with specifically in the debate earlier. It was not necessary to invoke those powers. The mere possession of those powers was sufficient to meet the needs of the situation that arose.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If that is the situation, will the minister give an example of how those powers helped the cotton mills in Cornwall?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was asked for a statement of what the government had done in relation to the textile industry. I have given that statement. I had some misgivings about being led into a debate on that question because the present amendment before the committee is only one of a number of things that the government has done in relation to this problem. I was asked what the other things were. I have dealt with them. With respect, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we could have a debate on this whole question of government policy and government administration but it will not relate to this present amendment before the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It will relate to it, as I hope to show in a moment, because I intend to go back to the debate and quote some of the statements made by the minister. I asked the minister whether he would give an example of how the legislation of 1958 actually assisted

Customs Tariff
or helped the mills in Cornwall, and his reply was, "I have already put on the record what the government has done to assist the textile industry generally". My comment on that statement is that notwithstanding all of the matters which the minister has put on record, a number of mills have closed elsewhere than in Cornwall. A mill closed in Hamilton. One closed in New Brunswick, in the area of Saint John: I have forgotten the name of the place but I think it is Milltown.
Was that not during the previous administration?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has referred to a statement I made on February 2. Here, of course, I had been speaking in general terms about the textile industry. I am quite sure the hon. member is aware that the Minister of National Revenue has made various orders, for instance, in relation to the definition of seconds. That is of general application, and I am sure that it must have had application, at least in part, to that section of the textile industry that was located in Cornwall.
The dumping provisions did not apply to seconds before that order was made by my colleague.

Mr. Chairman, the minister cannot really worm out of this quite so easily. 
He says here, as the hon. member for Laurier has just pointed out, that there had been an erosion over the past 10 years. To quote his words:
-and the erosion that has gone on over the past 10 years has gradually narrowed the power reposed in the government by parliament to deal with the dumping of goods of another nature that are of a class or kind made in Canada, and that applies to the textile goods made in those Cornwall mills.
When the minister says that the erosion applies to the textile goods made in the Cornwall mills, let the minister tell us what that erosion was. What were the decisions of the tariff board in these cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was not a reference to any decision of the tariff board. It was a reference to the effect of this course of decision. It affected everything that came within the scope of this problem of determining whether goods were of a class or kind made in Canada. It applied to everything. It applied to textiles, it applied to all sorts of goods and whether made in Cornwall or elsewhere. This erosion that had gone on had made it increasingly necessary, in order to bring the goods within the scope of the definition of class or kind made in Canada, to show that they were virtually identical with goods made in Canada.
That was the position in which the administration of the Department of National Revenue found itself as a result of this course of interpretation. This is a situation that affected everybody. This was the way in which the language that had been used by parliament, which had been given proper effect in the interpretations prior to the last decade, had been narrowed down as a result of this course of decision in the past decade, with effects on all Canadian producers in this field within the scope of some 75 items in the Canadian customs tariff. In particular, as I have pointed out already, the determination that goods are of a class or kind made in Canada is the basis for application of the dumping legislation. It has no application in any other case.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Mr. Chairman, in direct reply to what the minister has said, may I observe that to say in a pontifical way that this applies to all kinds of things does not make it apply. The minister said here quite specifically that it applies to textile goods made in these Cornwall mills and he was talking about the erosion that had taken place over the past ten years. Let the minister cite one single case where the customs department or the tariff board decided in the last ten

years that a textile that previously was considered to be made in Canada was no longer considered to be made in Canada. Let him cite one single case. Unless he can do so there is no erosion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the final observation of the hon. member is, of course, a complete non sequitur. He is trying again to identify decisions of the tariff board or the courts with the effects of the erosion. In the course of administration the department was not in a position to overlook the course of the decisions by the tariff board and the courts in narrowing down the interpretation and, of course, this situation had an effect on the administration. It could not be otherwise. The administration in the department cannot overlook or close its eyes to the results of this course of decision on the part of the tariff board and the courts over the past decade.
This matter has a very direct bearing upon textiles because it is the dumping provisions that are particularly to be invoked in the case of the dumping of textiles in Canada. Here is where the rub lay with respect to the textile field. I remind the house again, and I hope for the last time, Mr. Chairman, that the dumping provisions can be invoked only in the case of goods found to be of a class or kind made in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I asked the minister to give one example not of a decision by the tariff board but of a decision by the customs administration in the last ten years where they decided that any of the textiles that at any time had been made in Cornwall were no longer made in Canada. That is the only way there could be erosion.

May I ask a
question?
Surely the minister is going to answer before a diversion is created.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I recognize the hon. member for Stormont.

I should like to ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate a question. Since we are discussing the matter of worming out of things and since his colleague has wormed out of any answer to the question I asked him previously, let me ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the same question, namely whether he or any of his colleagues are in fact in favour of increasing the tariff on cottons in order to protect the textile industry in Canada. Are they or are they not in favour of it?

I will ask that question of the Minister of Finance right now. The
Customs Tariff
hon. gentleman has asked me a question and he can now sit down and let the minister answer.

I know the
minister's attitude and I asked my question of the member who is on his feet.

I do not happen to be a member of the government at the present time and I would not waste the time of the committee by answering the silly question asked by the hon. member for Stormont. I intend to put the question to the minister. Is this legislation, as the hon. member for Stormont is representing it to be, for the purpose of increasing protection?
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am not representing this legislation to be anything.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate has the floor at present and I would ask the hon. member for Stormont to seek his permission if the hon. member wants to speak.
I ask the minister, is this legislation for the purpose of increasing the tariff on textiles?
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, that is not the question I asked at all, and I should like an answer to my previous question. A direct answer, yes or no, will be sufficient.

The hon. member has no right to an answer to his question. He knows perfectly well what my views are but I am not even going to give him the satisfaction of an answer. I am asking the minister, who is mainly responsible for tariffs in this country at the present time and who is answerable to the house, is this legislation for the purpose of increasing the tariff on textiles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Obviously increases in tariffs do not enter into this situation at all.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I pointed out that this is a matter of definition-
I am quite satisfied with the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-and on the interpretation of the definition will depend whether the lower rate of duty applicable in the event that the goods are not of a class or kind made in Canada shall apply or whether in the relevant cases the higher customs tariff rates applicable in the event that the goods are of a class or kind made in Canada shall apply. That is the situation.

Customs Tariff
We are dealing with a definition, and so far as textile imports are concerned it is a question of whether the dumping provisions can be invoked.

I should like to ask the
minister another very simple and direct question. Does the minister know of any textile product made in Cornwall in the past ten years that was ever declared by the administration not to be made in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that
one cannot give a positive answer to that question because a good deal depends on a number of factors that do not admit of a categorical answer. Obviously textiles are in most cases shelf goods.
Then why on earth, when the minister now admits he does not know, did he tell us that the erosion applied to textiles made in Cornwall? Surely he had some facts on which to make that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope the hon. member is not going to misread my remarks. I was pointing out that this is of general application. This is of general application to the goods described in some 75 items in the customs tariff and this legislation deals with the definition of the term that appears in all of these provisions of the customs tariff. It has that general application and the erosion that has gone on in the past decade is an erosion applied to what had been a well established interpretation of those words prior to the last decade. The erosion that has gone on has weakened the effect of this definition as applied to all of these 70-odd items in the customs tariff. So far as textiles are concerned, the particular application relates to dumping because, and I hope I am saying this for the last time, the dumping provisions can be invoked only in the case of goods of a class or kind made in Canada. The application of dumping, therefore, depends upon the interpretation of those words appearing within the items.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister another question? Would this new definition concerning class or kind made in Canada apply to tariff item 413(i) which I understand provides for machinery or apparatus of a class or kind not made in Canada, and parts thereof, especially constructed for preparing, manufacturing, testing or finishing yarns, cordage and fabrics made from textile fibres or from paper, imported for use exclusively by manufacturers and scholastic or charitable institutions in such processes only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in an academic sense, if that is the basis of the question, certainly the expression "class
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).1
or kind", with which we are dealing does appear in item 413 (i) of the customs tariff and therefore the legislation will apply to that item. I am told, however, that no concrete case is likely to arise under that particular item.

I note the minister's appeal when he asked the members of the committee a little while ago to be reasonable. However, I find it rather difficult to understand his complaint against the submission of the hon. member for Assiniboia. The hon. member for Assiniboia claimed the government was asking for authority greatly to increase tariffs. A number of weeks ago the minister admitted this was the purpose of the legislation now before us. However, he has amended his contention now. I assume he has been around the country within the last few weeks and now he pleads, to use his own word, that the change is in the interests of better administration. He is asking that we restore the position of the Canadian producer because of the erosion that has taken place, as he likes to put it.
However, a couple of weeks ago he said the change was in the interests of protecting Canadian producers. Now he says it is in the interests of better administration. I find this alteration in his appeal a little difficult to understand. The minister made light of the amendment which would hand over to the Minister of National Revenue much more authority than he has had heretofore. The right to make law is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. We are being asked now to hand over to the government the right to interpret the law. I find this request rather difficult to appreciate. If I may use the minister's words again, he said we were concerned only with a question of definition. I feel that we are skating on rather thin ice when we are asked for authority to have a minister of the government replace the judiciary, and here we are granting the minister authority to define the law.
I feel that over the years the right to define the law has belonged to the judiciary. We are rather reinforced in our suspicions as a result of a speech made by the hon. member for Lincoln. I assume that this legislation went before a meeting of the Conservative members of this house on a Wednesday morning before it was introduced. The hon. member for Lincoln made some rather revealing announcements. He welcomed this legislation because, in his opinion, it would be much easier to get to the minister than to get to the tariff board. He complained that it was very difficult for ordinary members of this house to get to the tariff board. If I may use the hon. member's own words, to whom would it be better to go than

to the local member or the minister himself? In other words, political pressure is to be preferred to a decision of the tariff board. This is what alarms us more than anything else. The government is asking us to grant the Minister of National Revenue authority to interpret every definition in the interests of better administration. He is being granted authority to interpret the law, according to the words of the hon. member for Lincoln, in the light of the number of members of this house who may be running to him and appealing to him on behalf of a particular industry or commodity. I do not like to be placed in a position where I have to appeal to the minister to use his arbitrary powers on behalf of an industry in my constituency that may be in difficulties with the customs branch.
I should like to say a word or two about the submission of the hon. member for Laurier who pleaded for the Atlantic economic community in order, as I understood it, to help out the textile industry of Canada. The hon. member for Laurier also referred the Soviet competition. I ask the hon. member for Laurier to explain how Soviet competition or the development of the Atlantic economic community has anything to do with the difficulties of the textile industry in our nation today. I know this much; our textile industry does not face competition from the U.S.S.R. Indeed, most of the competition that faces our textile industry does not come from within the Atlantic economic community but comes from the mills of the United States and the United Kingdom. Therefore, when he proposes the establishment of the Atlantic economic community, he is not proposing any solution whatever for the problems of the cotton textile mills located in Ontario or Quebec. When he speaks of Soviet competition for the Canadian textile industry, he is not being relevant to the subject of the debate.
However, I should like to return to my earlier contention. When the minister introduced his baby budget, and for a number of weeks thereafter, he pleaded on behalf of Canadian secondary industries which had been eroded by decisions of the tariff board. During the weeks that have gone by, the minister has completely altered his argument on behalf of this legislation and he is now urging us to adopt this measure in the interests of better administration.
When we consider the authority that he is proposing to take away from the tariff board and hand over to the Minister of National Revenue I am afraid that we must oppose this resolution to the very limit of our abilities.
Customs Tariff

Mr. Chairman, in connection with the discussion this afternoon two things particularly interested me about the remarks made by the minister. When we were last discussing this resolution the minister made practically no comment. I believe he assumed that because, as he described it, it was a short resolution, and as such not worthy of debate. I think that the shortness of some declaratory resolutions as sometimes the shortness of individuals, is not in any way an indication of their dynamite potentials. I think the Minister of Finance would perhaps be the first to agree with that suggestion.
I should like to receive some direct information from the minister this afternoon. He gave us none the last time we discussed this subject. Surely he cannot expect to have it both ways; he cannot say that the legislation introduced in 1958 was never used, while on the other hand both he and representatives of his party travel up and down the land, particularly in textile ridings, saying that this legislation has been exceedingly helful to them. The minister himself, I believe in the middle of October 1960, addressed the Woollen and Knit Goods Manufacturing Association in his usual vigorous declaratory style saying: "Our actions have been swift, comprehensive and effective". The Minister of National Revenue, with respect to any changes in the Customs Tariff such as we have referred to, now says the amendments of 1958 have not been used. The minister has not yet replied to the hon. member for Laurier who has asked: What has the government done by this legislation that has helped the textile industry?
The second point I should like to make is this, and I regret that I have to go back to the points I raised a week or so ago in regard to the question of erosion. The minister again relies on assertions rather than facts. He says there has been erosion. Without repeating everything I said last week, I would ask the minister to give us illustrations, something concrete in regard to the decisions of the tariff board during the last decade about which he complains or decisions which have gone contrary to what the bureaucrats themselves said was the law. In one case, appeal No. 272 in connection with shovels, I indicated that the bureaucrats were upheld when the tariff board said that their judgment was correct in administering the customs department. A few days after that decision was given the bureaucrats changed their traditional ruling and then met the second appeal, No. 306. Of course, in that case the tariff board overruled the administration.

Customs Tariff
Let us get down to cases rather than just accept a statement from the Minister of Finance that there has been erosion. Let us have the Minister of Finance indicate to us the cases he regards as the ones which change the intent of parliament as it was enacted prior to a decade ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks before the house arises because I know that at eight o'clock the minister has other engagements and that we will be dealing with the resolution to establish a committee on railways and shipping.
I am quite disappointed, as I am sure were the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate and the hon. member for Kenora-Kainy River, in the statement the minister made in answer to questions put by us from this side of the house. I was disappointed in the reply the minister made in his earlier statement of February 2 when he said that this erosion applied to the Cornwall mills. When he was asked about a concrete example he could not give one of that erosion I think the minister should reply to that question giving us an example of this erosion of which he spoke when he made the statement earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this information was fully given and is on the record. This information was put on the record by the Minister of National Revenue, and myself on February 2 at very great length.

The minister is undoubtedly referring to his skirting the question and his very unusual interpretation in doing so in respect to the number of cases over the past decade to which he referred. If the minister is not going to reply at this point, having dealt with two of these appeals, I am now prepared to deal with each and every one and indicate my reading of the tariff board decisions. In practically all cases not only did the tariff board uphold what the administration said was law, but it upheld the law as it had been for many years prior to 1950. This is the challenge which we put before the Minister of Finance. We are not asking him to persuade colleagues in his own party that all is serene in connection with this amended law and is not going to convince us. We challenge him to indicate to us details with respect to the erosion which he so frequently asserts has taken place.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: RAILWAYS. AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved:
subtopic: RAILWAYS. AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That a sessional committee on railways, airlines and shipping owned and controlled by the government be appointed to consider the accounts, estimates and bills relating to the Canadian National Railway and Trans-Canada Air Lines, saving always the power of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public monies, and to consider the pension rights of existing or retired Canadian National Railway employees with respect to anomalies which may have resulted from breaks in the continuity of service, and also to consider the arrangements for turn around benefits for employees of the Canadian National Railway, and the said committee should be empowered to send for persons, papers and records and to report from time to time, and that notwithstanding standing order 67, the said committee shall consist of twenty six members.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have a very short statement to make. This motion is to appoint a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government.
As the house knows, it has been the practice for many years to appoint a committee to review the affairs of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines.
In due course, when the annual reports of the two companies have been received and tabled in the house, they will be referred to the committee together with the items of estimates that are customarily considered by the committee. As hon. members are aware, these reports are usually ready during the month of March.
Hon. members will have noted that this year the terms of reference of the committees have been expanded to permit consideration of the pension rights of existing or retired Canadian National Railway employees with respect to anomalies which may have resulted from breaks in the continuity of service, and also to consider the arrangements for turn-around benefits for employees of the Canadian National Railways.
When speaking on the bill to provide for the continuance of railway operations the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that the government would ask that an investigation be undertaken into the objections that have been raised over the years that turn-around benefits have not been properly provided and that pensions had been adversely affected by lay-offs due to economic

conditions, particularly during the 1930's. This motion provides for such an investigation.
This committee has always proved its value and I am sure that with the added terms of reference its deliberations will again be conducted with the same thoroughness and efficiency that has characterized its proceedings in the past.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: RAILWAYS. AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The house will be grateful to the minister for the statement he has just made, although some of us may think it was brief in nature. I presume the intention in making it brief is to curtail the extent of the discussion on this motion.
I do not intend to deal with this resolution at great length but there are some things which I think need to be said on the occasion of this discussion. The motion as it appears on the order paper is divided into two parts. It seeks, first of all, to establish a committee to consider the accounts, estimates and bills of two crown corporations, namely the Canadian National Railways and the Trans-Canada Air Lines. Second, it seeks the permission of the house for a study to be made of the pension rights of existing or retired employees of Canadian National Railways. This, of course, brings up at once a number of matters which affect both crown corporations.
It will not, of course, be news to the house to learn either from the annual report of the C.N.R., through the minister or through the president of the C.N.R. that the financial position of Canadian National Railways has really worsened. This is not only in the field of freight but also in the field of passenger service. I think one had some intimation of this situation as far back as the report of the royal commission on transportation made by Mr. Justice Turgeon and two of his colleagues in 1951. A careful glance at the recommendations of that report gives some indication that there are a number of factors affecting the operation of the Canadian National Railways and, I suppose I can say, railways in general. One of these factors is the inroads made by aviation into the field of rail transportation and another is the increase in the size of the trucking industry. The motor car and truck and the aeroplane have made tremendous inroads into freight and railway passenger business, this notwithstanding the many innovations which have been introduced by both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
In 1960 I believe the deficit of the Canadian National Railways may well be the largest in its history. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) brought down his baby budget
Railways and Shipping Committee in December I believe he gave some indication of what the deficit of the Canadian National Railways might be. It was certainly of the order of $75 million.
The railway position in the United Kingdom and in the United States is not unlike that in our own country. Railway expansion in the United States has not kept pace with the increase in population but rather has fallen behind, giving way especially before the advance of the motor truck and the aeroplane in almost every part of the United States. That statement is applicable to our own railways in Canada. Then we had the establishment of a royal commission in 1959 to deal with railway matters. That commission, now known as the MacPherson commission, was charged with a number of problems, two of which were the inequities in the freight rate structure and the obligations and limitations imposed upon railways by law for reasons of public policy.
I think it would be interesting to the house to learn from the minister, when he replies, what is the position of the present royal commission on transportation. When will it report? The Prime Minister in a previous debate stated that the royal commission is expected to recommend a method of freight increases which will prevent discriminatory rates. At the time of the debate regarding the resumption of work of railway employees it was said that the report would be handed down by March 31 this year. That date is coming fairly soon; it is the end of next month. Is this result still going to be possible? Notwithstanding the delays that have been occasioned in the hearing of evidence and in the presentation of briefs since the debate on the railway issue, is the royal commission on transportation still going to be able to meet the schedule that was referred to at that time? Until January of this year the royal commission was still hearing witnesses and only recently has this procedure ceased.
The next point is this. When will the discussion on the briefs take place? Assuming that this discussion were to end during the month of February, this would barely give the commission three months in which to write a report of tremendous importance. As the house knows, the Turgeon report on transportation was handed down after many months of study not only by the chairman of this commission but also by his colleagues. I know from experience that it would have been impossible for Mr. Justice Turgeon to hand down a report in three months on a matter of this magnitude and importance. The matters that have been submitted to the royal commission on transportation are not unlike, certainly in importance, those that were submitted to the royal commission in
2468	HOUSE OF
Railways and Shipping Committee 1951. Therefore, the question I ask is this. How can the commission in the short time at its disposal have a report of this importance ready by March 31?
I think the minister also might well give some consideration to another matter that has been engaging the attention of the house from time to time. I refer to the question of lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. What is the position with reference to this matter? I know from experience that the officers of the Canadian National Railways hesitate to give information on this subject not only to the minister but also to the house.
I am not going to debate the propriety of this situation, but I think the minister should take the opportunity to indicate to the house what has been the position with reference to these lay-offs. It has been stated from time to time that about 5,000 employees per year have been laid off by the C.N.R. within the last three or four years. If that is the case, that would be about 20,000 employees.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RAILWAYS. AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Order. May I mention to the hon. member that in my view he is straying away from the subject matter of the motion before the house. This motion does not permit, to my mind, a general discussion on the problems of transportation or on all the problems which concern the C.N.R.
I do not wish to limit the hon. member but he realizes that if I permit him to speak on all these matters in which he may be interested I shall be obliged to allow the same latitude to all other hon. members. Generally speaking, on a motion to set up a committee the only questions which are relevant are those mentioned in the motion, and specially the expediency of setting up a committee. As the minister knows, this afternoon I raised a question concerning air routes. I turn now to another aspect of this committee's work, namely a study of the operations of the crown corporation known as Trans-Canada Air Lines. In so far as our air carriers and our air lines are concerned, there is a fairly serious situation with reference to fifth freedom rights. The Financial Post carried a story to the effect that an examiner of the civil aeronautics board of the United States had recommended to that board the granting of permission to two United States air lines to fly Toronto to Miami via Buffalo and Toronto to Washington and Philadelphia via Buffalo without any corresponding rights being given to Canadian air carriers. At the committee hearings I think the minister should tell us what is being done by the government
Railways and Shipping Committee to offset this serious situation because there can be no doubt that tremendous harm is being done to our air lines.
These are questions that come to my mind now. This consideration raises the whole question of the income position of the Trans-Canada Air Lines. Certainly he also stated that one can discuss general heads of discussion such as the regional divisions of the C.N.R., as I did; lay-offs on the C.N.R.; curtailment of operations; the royal commission on transportation; Trans-Canada Air Lines; and, in a general way, the air agreements that affect the profit and loss position of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
I think it was also stated that such a discussion should authorize a review of matters that are of urgent importance and cannot be debated prior to the meeting of the committee. Railways and Shipping Committee was stated by Trans-Canada Air Lines and also by the minister, I believe, that employment would be found for all of these men. Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply briefly to the argument just introduced by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
It is a well known fact that retired C.N.R. workers have been urging the government of Canada since 1945 to increase the pensions paid to former employees of the so-called government owned railways such as the Intercolonial Railway and others in eastern Canada. Since my election to the House of Commons I have consistently placed a resolution in this
Railways and Shipping Committee regard on the order paper. The resolution that was placed on the order paper this year appeared on November 24 and is No. 38 under routine proceedings of this date. This resolution urges the government once again, for the third consecutive session, to introduce legislation providing for an increase in pensions paid to railway employees.
I submit that the proposed amendment is out of order. It is designed to confuse and to put responsibility on a sessional committee to examine the pension privileges of employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway and other railways. I am certain that the interpretation of the minister's resolution would be one which would include not only the Canadian National Railways but certain railways in eastern and western Canada formerly owned or controlled by the government. This resolution would include the right of the committee to examine pensions of various railway companies owned and controlled by the government. I think it would only add confusion and delay and create impossible results for a small committee of 26 members to attempt to determine what pensions railway workers outside of government owned or controlled lines should be entitled to.
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that all railway workers are included in this resolution if they worked for railways controlled by the government. They are automatically included because in 1922 the Canadian National Railways took over government-controlled railways. The amendment is unnecessary as far as I am concerned.
I should like to see this committee formed, and I have every reason to expect that it will make a thorough investigation into existing hardships. I am sure that the hardships of former employees of government railways will be considered together with inequities which exist, if any, under the current C.N.R. regulations on pensions. I therefore suggest that the point of order is ill-founded. I also suggest that the amendment is unnecessary because it does nothing but add confusion and impossibilities to the task of the committee.
