Railways and Shipping Committee the Prime Minister made in this house. The commitment appears at page 356 of Hansard and reads as follows:

Mr. Speaker, we may not win many votes but at least tonight we win the attendance contest. On May 5 two years ago Clark Davey of the Globe and Mail had the following story reporting on the sessional committee on railways:
C.N.R. President Donald Gordon bluntly told members of parliament today that if there is a strong feeling the government owned railway is not being efficiently operated he and his top management team should be fired.

I intend at some time in the committee's proceedings to see what support I can And to take Mr. Gordon at his word because I have reached the stage where it is my view that he has about reached the end of the road as president of Canadian National Railways, and I should like to go on and make some points as to why I feel this is so.
As everyone knows, the head of Canadian National Railways, namely Mr. Gordon, is a very blunt, outspoken, forthright man. He is prepared to take his chances as can be judged by his statement, "If you do not think we are efficient, fire us". In every year that Mr. Gordon has been before the committee when I have been a member of it he has emphasized that he wants Canadian National Railways to be treated as a private enterprise organization with a balance sheet and all its efficiencies. I do not think that is what Canadian National Railways should be but if that is what Mr. Gordon thinks it is, and if that is what he insists his instructions from parliament are, then on that basis I think Mr. Gordon must go. He has had his decade in charge of Canadian National Railways and it seems to me that all he has accomplished every year is a bigger and bigger spending program and in most cases a bigger and bigger deficit. I know that the morale of the railway employees has nosedived and there seem to be no future prospects for efficiency or for any kind of balanced budget on the Canadian National Railways as long as we have Mr. Gordon as the president of the railway.
There is one thing about Mr. Gordon. He does not want only himself to tumble if the railway is found guilty of inefficiency. He thinks his top staff should go too. From what I hear in my constituency in which there are many railroaders there are a great many top staff on the Canadian National Railways. I had a report the other day with regard to one particular place where there used to be a balanced work force and now there are more foremen than there are employees. There seem to be a great many chiefs and very few Indians on the Canadian National Railways. When it comes to determining how many chiefs are to go along with Mr. Gordon I think the committee should investigate this matter and should try to question him when he is before us as to just who he thinks should depart with him if the committee finds, as I think it should, that he is inefficient and that the top management have been inefficient.
There is one thing that has intrigued me about Mr. Gordon. He has worked out a technique that I think most politicians should use. You might call it blunt candour. He is always ready to admit the worst right at the

Railways and Shipping Committee first. I noticed that a couple of weeks ago he made a speech entitled "Total Distribution Costs". He was addressing the Canadian industrial traffic league in Toronto on February 16 and through some kind of courtesy I have a copy of his speech tonight. He said:

I have told you of my concern about the inability of the railway industry to hold its share of the transportation market despite very large capital expenditures to improve every phase of its physical operation.
He is being very candid with us. Every year he comes along and asks for more money. Every year we have a generally increasing deficit. However, Mr. Gordon has always taken us into his confidence. He says that in the future things are going to improve but in ten years they never have improved. The situation has deteriorated.
My interest in the railway situation, of course, stems from the fact that the employees are complaining very much about the situation. They have lost faith in the present management. Morale is shot, and all you have to do is to look at the changes in the employment structure and the number of jobs that are disappearing. All you have to do is to visit some of the divisional points to see just how serious things are. Mr. Gordon went on to say:
I have explained why the Canadian National decided that a physical rejuvenation alone was not enough and how we have undertaken a major organizational overhaul.
This is the point I want to make as a reason why we should consider that Mr. Gordon is inefficient and that it is time he should go. He has been there for ten years and finally at long last out of a clear blue sky he has plucked this terrific change about which we are all hearing.

My point is that Mr. Gordon has introduced now a sweeping reorganization of Canadian National Railways. Maybe it is a good one but the three great moves he has made in connection with the railway have indicated to me that he is not in control and cannot direct the destinies of this railway to the best advantage.
Hon. members who have been in the house for some time will recall that the big thing Mr. Gordon wanted to do when he took over Canadian National Railways was to get the debt position of that railway straightened out. Canadian National Railways had to earn a tremendous amount of money for interest charges on a debt for which it was really not originally responsible. Some adjustment was made in the early fifties with regard to this debt position. It was all cleared up and Canadian National Railways no longer had this onerous debt burden. In a way, that was Mr. Gordon's first big ploy.
The second big ploy concerned a tremendous capital input in order to get modern diesel locomotives for the Canadian National Railways. The dieselization program has been completed and most of the railway has been modernized in so far as its signal organization is concerned. Two large humpyards have been put into operation, and a couple more

will soon be working. I would not doubt that these improvements have had some considerable effect on the efficiency of the Canadian National Railways. However, they have not brought Canadian National Railways any closer to the kind of balance sheet that Mr. Gordon insisted should be expected from Canadian National Railways. We are no closer to a balanced operation, no closer to a profit position. In other words, Mr. Gordon has failed in his private enterprise direction.
We are now hearing a great deal about the administrative overhaul of the system and the development of a new symbol. This appears to me to be another method of carrying Mr. Gordon for a couple of years, another excuse for delay. I feel that after 10 years Mr. Gordon and those close to him have had their chance. I do not agree that we should consider the Canadian National Railways as a private enterprise. Those are the terms under which Mr. Gordon insists he should operate. I would argue-and our party takes this view-that the whole railway operation in Canada should be consolidated under a government corporation. We feel that almost all railway organizations in Canada today have to receive some form of subsidy. We feel that railway operations need some common plan.

I should like to know why this whole pension question is not being studied as it relates to all railways. It seems to me that was the undertaking the Prime Ministre gave. I think the Minister of Transport should explain this change to us before we pass this resolution.
I know that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River feels this offer of the Prime Minister's was a red herring. I must say that was my own opinion. I felt that it was designed to take the edge off much of the bitterness amongst railway employees. I certainly feel that this resolution is not broad enough to permit the problem to be properly tackled. Those members who follow railroad history will know that some years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway fired a number of

Railways and Shipping Committee employees. Those employees finally got back on the railroad, but their years of service before the firing took place were not recognized for pension purposes. A battle has been fought on this subject by members of parliament for many years, and some success has been attained, but never complete success. This break in service as it applies to pension rights has been one of the big issues, and if we are going to look at the pension situation of Canadian National employees it seems to me the same people should be looking at the pension situation of Canadian Pacific employees. Otherwise, the Prime Minister's promise really becomes a half-hearted one or an incomplete one. I hear one hon. member say, "as usual". What we should be considering at this time in relation to the committee's operations is the impact of automation and the response of the railway to this situation. During the years I have been a member of the committee, Mr. Gordon has always given us grand assurances that the railway is responding to the challenge of automation by providing for the movement of personnel and job training. However, when it comes to the point of giving, the details, he will not provide the details. At this point he always begins another favourite gambit which is part of that candour he exhibits and which usually strikes some response from some members of the committee. He begins to play up the bogey of the labour unions and the contract agreements the railways have with the unions. He has told all the members of parliament that they should keep their noses out of these employee matters because a good arrangement has been worked out in the contracts between the management and the unions.
However, when you ask Mr. Gordon for the details of this job training program and the shifts, he says something about the 27 unions with which the railway has contracts; they all have different jurisdictions, different geographical boundaries, and so it is very difficult to get moving. As a consequence, these union people keep coming to members of parliament rather than going through union channels because it seems that neither does Mr. Gordon nor do the unions know what the channels are. I can give you a prime example of just what took place last year. With nine days' notice Mr. Gordon's officials notified the running trades at North Bay, Nakina and


Hornepayne that a new freight service there was going to be put in operation a new freight service that would require them to cover two divisions rather than one. These men arrived in Ottawa and asked their M.P's what they were going to do about this situation. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) and I, being the members of parliament involved, had great difficulty in receiving answers to questions which we asked the officials involved. We received standard responses such as: "It will take some while to consider these things".
I remember asking these railroaders from North Bay, Nakina and Hornepayne what their unions were going to do about this situation. They replied that there was nothing that could be done because this service was to be introduced very quickly. They asked me what I would advise them to do. I advised them to pull a wildcat strike. I told them that was the only thing to do in a situation like this. They did not have to pull a wildcat strike. All they had to do was to threaten to do so. The proposed change was postponed and a more satisfactory basis was worked out. I should like to inform hon. members why I advised these people to pull a wildcat strike. I advised them to do so because I felt it was the only way in which they could get the attention and action of the officials.
A proposed change such as the one I have described involves much more than just the railway. This change involved the community situation of towns such as North Bay, Nakina, and Hornepayne. Perhaps 20 or 30 families would be required to shift very quickly and arbitrarily in order to find work in this situation. Everyone would be prepared to make changes in jobs and in working conditions under certain circumstances. However, what happened last year when Mr. Gordon appeared before this sessional committee? Mr. Gordon assured us that in the future, as a result of the complaints of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and other members of parliament, there would not be as drastic or as serious a change made in the Canadian National Railway which would have great effects upon the community without the community involved being taken into the confidence of the railway officials. What do we now find as a result of this assurance? We received nine days' notice of the change. That is the way in which the Canadian National Railway management appears to operate in carrying out the undertakings and promises that the president has made so readily before this parliamentary committee.
I hope other hon. members will join with me during the proceedings of this committee this year in pointing out to Mr. Gordon that it is felt he did not meet the challenge two

years ago, and in asking him why he should not be fired immediately. I feel that we shall have a most interesting committee this year. I feel that the members of parliament as members of that committee will not be bullied, browbeaten or pushed around by Mr. Gordon. I do not feel they have been so treated while I have been a member of that committee in spite of the interpretation that has been placed upon Mr. Gordon's activities before that committee in the past.
I should like to speak on another point that we have always found unsatisfactory. I am sure that there are other members as well as myself who are anxious to have the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway appear before the committee. We have never been able to get from the officials of the Canadian National Railway an acceptable statement in regard to its co-operation with the Canadian Pacific Railway officials, something which, of course, is required under a statute which has appeared on the books for a long time. We are always put off with just a little information and the answer that the Canadian Pacific Railways officials do consult with the officials of the Canadian National Railway. There does exists a statute which instructs the Canadian National Railway officials to co-operate, to pool services and to make sincere efforts to get along. Mr. Gordon is never prepared to go so far as to say anything more than that this procedure does take place. We see little evidence of this pooling of services and co-operation. It is for these reasons that I should like to see Mr. Crump appear before this committee so that we could hear his side of the situation in regard to the relationship between the two railways in respect of cooperation. There is no kidding about the fact that Mr. Crump and Mr. Gordon are real buddies when they get together against the railway workers. This fact is shown in the speech that Mr. Gordon made to the industrial traffic league. This is ironical to members of parliament because there is a comparison of like with like. The unions are using a yardstick that the railways in one of their cooperative moments worked out.

speechtext: Tomorrow we will commence with item No. 15 on today's order paper, a resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister referring to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. PORTUGAL COVE-BELL ISLAND FERRY, NFLD.-LANDING FACILITIES
speechtext:
What is the result of the investigation referred
to by the Minister of Transport in his answer to starred question No. 20 on November 30, 1960?
Answer by; Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport):
Existing terminal facilities for the ferry John Guy were found to be unsatisfactory. Temporary repairs and modifications of the terminals have been authorized at an estimated cost of $87,175 and work will be started immediately.
